To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

we have generated a new MDCK-II cell model to study the function of bovine ABC transporter ABCG2 and that this model can be used to identify new substrates of ABCG2 and to study the pharmacological activity of ABCG2.
we generated new MDKII cell models stabling expressing the wild-type and Y551S variants of bovine ABC2 and we identified new bovine ABC2 substrates, including fluoroquinolones.

we have established a new in vitro cell model using MDCKII stably expressing bovin ABCG2 (wild-type and Y581 variant) to study ABCG 2-mediated transcellular transport of xenobiotic compounds across a physiologic barrier.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the development and application of new in vitro and in silico tools to improve our understanding of the mechanisms involved in xenobiotic transport across physiological barriers and in the design of novel drug formulations and drug delivery systems.

the development of new in vitro models to investigate drug disposition and pharmacokinetics in the mammary gland of lactating cows and other dairy species, and to study the mechanisms underlying drug secretion into milk.
the development of new in vitro models for functional studies of ABC transporters in the lactating dairy cow, including ABCG1, ABCG2 and ABCC1.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
no adequate in vitro cell model is yet available to study the transport of xenobiotic compounds across the blood-mammary barrier of ruminant species.
no suitable in vitro model has been developed to investigate ABCG 2-mediated transport of substrates across the physiologic blood-milk barrier.
“no suitable model has been developed yet to study ABCG 2-mediated transport across physiologically normal barriers”.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have generated for the first-time an adequate in vitro cell model that allows us to study ABCG1- and ABCG2-mediated drug transport across the physiological mammary gland barrier of dairy animals.

“In this work, we have generated for the first, to the best our knowledge, suitable in vitro models for the normal blood–milk barrier using MDKII cells expressing bovin or caprin ABCG2” and “We have developed the first in vitro model of the bovine blood–milk and caprine blood–milk barriers to study ABCG 2-mediated transport of substrates”.
we were the first to establish an in vitro cell model using MDCKII expressing bovine ABC2G to study drug transport across a physiological blood-milk barrier.
The main takeaway from our work is that
we generated a suitable in vitro system to study ABCG1-mediated transport across a barrier using MDCK II cells expressing bovine (wild-type and Y581 variant) ABCG2.
MDCKII cells can be used to investigate the transport of xenobiotic substrates across a physiological barrier.
we generated for the first-time suitable in vitro cell models to investigate the ABCG2-mediated secretion of xenobiotics and toxins into milk of dairy ruminants.
